hero_deck: Lima Airport had never charged international transfer passengers a fee. I designed and tested the web prototype to collect it.
hero_role1: Roles — Innovation Specialist · UX/UI designer · CX designer
hero_role3: Scope — Planning → UX/UI design → prototyping → evaluation → handoff
hero_rv_txt: As Innovation specialist, I designed the TUUA Transfer web payment flow to solve the lack of a fee collection channel for connecting passengers, working with the airport's central departments. Today, the implemented system successfully collects this fee from over 130,000 international transfer passengers each month.
act0_lede: How a payment affects the experience during a connecting flight.
act0_pos_btn: Two ways to pay the fee
act0_pos_txt: A physical-digital model. The fee is paid inside the airport, mid-connection. Three staffed points carry most payments, issuing a bar-code sticker for the boarding pass. A web channel, exclusive to this fee, lets passengers skip peak-hour queues with a QR. Both end at the eGate.
act1_verdict: A fee with no way to collect it.
act1_lede: Five moments from concession to collection, and the income at stake.
act1_t1_x: LAP begins operating Jorge Chávez under concession with Peruvian State.
act1_t2_x: Amendment N°6 allows transfer fees upon delivery of new terminal.
act1_t3_x: The fee becomes chargeable, but no mechanism exists to collect it.
act1_t4_x: LAP and Airlines negotiated fee collection inside the ticket.
act1_t5_x: Implementation of fee mechanism at the airport, led by LAP Finance.
act1_s3_p: The Peruvian State takes 46.5% as royalty.
act1_est_txt: 130,000 × $10.05 ÷ 30 days. $10.05 is the fee before 18% IGV, which makes it $11.86. Lima Airport keeps 53.489%; the State takes 46.511% as royalty under the concession. An estimate at today's volume, not a measured loss.

act3_l1_x: Passenger side: data capture, card payment, and an e-receipt with an eGate QR. Back office: sales reports reconciled with gateway and real-time sync with airport's fee system, sized for 4 million+ passengers a year.
act3_l2_x: E-payments confirmed in real time, returning the data for e-receipt and access QR. PCI DSS certified, 99.9% availability and peaks of 1,500 transactions an hour, with daily reconciliation and chargeback reports.
act3_l3_x: Four mobile screens: personal data, email code, card payment and the QR ticket for the eGate. A clickable version of the same flow carried the stakeholder review.
act3_l4_x: Three models of e-payment in transport put initial web adoption at 5% of int-int passengers. Demand was split across web, cash desks, eGate POS, and mobile POS, so PlanOps could size counters and queues.
act3_l5_x: A service blueprint of the payment experience, differentiating tasks made by passenger, front-office, back-office, and the automated ones.

act6_lede: Five live steps, each set against my proposal.

act6_v2_x: A click instead of an automatic check

act6_method: Public, unauthenticated pages only. No transaction submitted, no data sent.
act6_note1: My participation. I understand the platform's mechanism and contributed to its UX/UI design — not its development, deployment or operation. Work testimony available upon formal request.
act6_note2: What's next: a lower fee, inside the ticket. In July 2026, LAP proposed cutting the fee from $10.05 to $6.40 + IGV and moving it into the ticket. Airlines haven't agreed; collection in the terminal continues.
act6_note3: My stance on the fee. Designing its collection channel doesn't make me a party to the fee itself. Whether it continues is for Peru's Judiciary to decide: in June 2026, a Lima court allowed a constitutional challenge to proceed, while collection continues.
